speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN MAIL DELIVERIES TO SERVICE PERSONNEL IN KOREA
speechtext:
On
Friday last, the hon. member for Prince Albert asked me a question seeking information about the delivery of mail in Korea. Today the hon. member for Greenwood called my office seeking similar information. Since speaking on Friday last to the hon. member for Prince Albert, I have had inquiries made in regard to mail service to the troops in Korea and am advised that there has been no justifiable cause for complaints. I have also had inquiries made at the Department of National Defence and have received a similar reply.
I thought that hon. members would like to know also that up to the present it has been possible to forward all letter mail by air, whether prepaid for air or surface transmission. It so happens that the necessary extra space has been available on the aircraft, and advantage has been taken of it to transport surface letters as well by that means. Records show that it generally takes from three to six days for this mail, which is dispatched three times per week from Vancouver, to reach the troops. It naturally takes longer for parcels. They are dispatched on an average once a week, with a transmission time of about one month. The elapsed time will vary, depending on whether or not the parcel makes a good connection with the transport.
We are confident that the mail service to the troops in Korea is operating on a sound basis, but I would like to assure the hon. members that if they know of any specific instances where mail has been unreasonably delayed, and will give me the facts, I shall be glad to have a detailed inquiry made and take any corrective measures that may be possible.

The house resumed, from Monday, March 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for committee of supply.

Mr. Speaker, by ancient usage and time-honoured custom an opportunity is granted any private member who has a grievance, or who feels that an injustice has been done to any private citizen, to bring this to the attention of the government and the house before supply is passed. I have such a grievance which I wish to place before the house at this time.
On July 7 of last year the Seaboard Shipping Company of British Columbia notified the immigration officers in Vancouver that a certain Polish seaman had deserted from a vessel of theirs, which was known as the Nordpol. At the same time the captain of the Nordpol notified the immigration authorities at Chemainus, British Columbia, that this seaman had deserted. The seaman's name was Richard Nowalinski.
Richard Nowalinski on the following day reported to the immigration officer in Victoria. There he explained the situation to the officer. He was granted a conditional release on a bond of $1,000 being placed on his behalf
[Mr. Claxton 1
by the president of the Catholic Women's League of Victoria, and other people who are interested in looking after the welfare of new Canadians arriving in this country. As a result of this bond being deposited, Richard Nowalinski was able to obtain employment as chief engineer on one of the vessels of the Victoria Tug Company Limited, he having become an experienced engineer and one familiar with diesel engines in Poland before arriving in this country.
The order for deportation was eventually passed and was subsequently appealed by Richard Nowalinski, the Roman Catholic bishop of Victoria and other people supporting that appeal. Mr. W. McGregor, managing director of the Victoria Tug Company, reported that this man's work had been eminently satisfactory, and offered him a permanent position with that company.
However, on the request from the Seaboard Shipping Company in a letter signed by Mr. E. J. Moller of that company to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in Vancouver, Nowalinski was tranferred to Vancouver. The request was made in these words:
Please arrange to have him-
That is Richard Nowalinski.
-transferred to your Vancouver jail at your earliest convenience.
That was dated July 22, 1953. That Polish seaman remained in the Vancouver jail of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, in spite of numerous protests by various people, until the 31st day of December, 1953, when, at almost a moment's notice, he was hurried away from Vancouver under police escort, was sent across to Vancouver island, and on to Port Alberni, where he was placed on board another vessel and was shipped out of the country.
The unusual circumstances of a man who apparently had only two crimes against him, one that of leaving a ship, and the other of hatred of communism and a determination to get away from behind the iron curtain, were brought to my attention at the end of last year and caused a great deal of interest on the Pacific coast. When it was found that an order had been issued for his deportation and that an appeal was made, a form known as immigration form 55 was signed as an application by two people, Mrs. W. Rogers, who is head of the Catholic women's group looking after immigrants coming to this country, and Mr. William McGregor, managing director of the Victoria Tug Company, asking that Richard Nowalinski be granted permission to come to this country and reside here.

After giving a brief description of his illegal entry into Canada and explaining that he worked as chief engineer on board a tug owned by the applicant's company, before being sent over to Vancouver, the application then went on to say:
The applicant therefore knows-
That is, the managing director of Victoria Tug Company.
-the proposed immigrant personally and knows his qualifications, and is most anxious to obtain his services, as it is impossible to find replacement for this man in this area.
The report goes on to say:
Representations have apparently been made to the minister by the local Roman Catholic bishop and Mr. McGregor.
And then, in the words of the immigration official who took this submission:
This application is submitted at this time as the applicant feels that since the proposed immigrant is a refugee and cannot obtain a valid passport from any country, he will be unable to land at any port to make application on his own behalf for admission to Canada.
Then the application goes on to say that the settlement arrangements are satisfactory, and this is signed by the immigration officer and approved by Mr. J. McDonald, acting immigration officer in charge at Victoria.
However, at the request of the shipping company, this man was taken from the employment where he was earning money and his own keep, and carrying out a useful job, and was placed in jail in Vancouver. That was in July of last year. From his cell in the immigration jail he wrote to various people soliciting their help. Amongst those to whom he wrote was the president of the United Nations. He set out his case, and that appeal was eventually sent to the immigration branch here in Ottawa. The appeal is given in the letter which Nowalinski wrote to the United Nations' office. The office of the high commissioner for refugees outlines the experiences which this unfortunate man had after he escaped from Poland in order to avoid the penalties which an anti-communist might expect in a country behind the iron curtain. He wrote not only on behalf of himself, but on behalf of two other immigrants, one a Yugoslav and the other another Pole who were then also in the immigration office jail at Vancouver.
This is his letter to the president of the United Nations:
We are respectfully approaching you with a request for the help of the United Nations, as we do not know to whom or to where we should properly apply. We are political refugees from Poland and Yugoslavia, and would like to know whether the so-called right of asylum actually exists, and if so, where we have to apply for it.
Deportation of Polish Seaman
I have so far sought it many times, in Sweden, Norway, Belgium, Egypt, England and now Canada, but all those countries categorically turned me down.
1 fled from Poland on a Swedish ship in 1949, and am to this very day without the right to stay in any country at all. From the Swedish boat I took refuge in Egypt, where I asked for asylum. This was refused, and I spent three months in prison there, after which I was put on a Finnish boat. When I arrived in the United Kingdom, the local immigration authorities put me in prison, where I spent fourteen days before being returned to the boat I had arrived on. On reaching Belgium, I discovered that the boat was bound for Poland, so I naturally ran away, and reported to the police in Antwerp, asking whether I could stay in Belgium. They arrested me and I spent another two months in prison, after which they put me on a Norwegian boat. Arriving in Norway several months later, I applied to the local authorities for the right to stay in that country, but. of course, met with refusal. After six weeks in prison, they packed me off on another Norwegian boat, on which I spent two years.
In the meantime, I wrote on several occasions to the immigration authorities in Norway and to IRO in Paris, likewise receiving negative replies. At the moment, we are being detained by the immigration authorities in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, for being in Canada illegally.
As we have never been punished for criminal offences, we cannot understand why, or for how long, we must continue to wander like vagabonds over the face of the earth and lodge in prisons all over the world.
At the time of the German invasion, we fought in defence of our country's freedom, and I personally served for three years in the Polish army.
The current political situation is such that it is absolutely impossible for us to return to our homeland. Yet no one else will take us in.
Accordingly, we respectfully ask the United Nations to examine our difficult position, as there is no other authority which is willing to take an interest in us or to look into our circumstances.
As none of us have a valid passport, it is impossible for us to seek legal entry or immigration into any country whatsoever. All we want is to be able to find a permanent home and work, no matter where. We would like to mention that our ages range from 25 to 32, and that we are skilled workers, and do not wish to spend our lives wandering all over the place in ships.
We are human beings, and as such are surely entitled to settle down in a free country, and to stay and work there. We earnestly beg the United Nations once again to consider our difficult plight, and await your favourable reply very anxiously, but also very hopefully.
That letter was sent on with the request that this man's condition be inquired into. It was pointed out that the purpose of writing was to urge that the case be given every consideration and to state that if an investigation disclosed that these persons were worthy of help the international rescue committee would be willing to provide them with some financial assistance. It would also be glad to contact some voluntary or ethnic societies in Vancouver to solicit their assistance in finding jobs. The letter goes on to state:
We have already contacted the Polish Canadian congress with this object in view.
Nowalinski was retained, as I have already pointed out, for this incredibly long time in

Deportation of Polish Seaman the jail in Vancouver. The reason given for his retention all that time was that the ship which had brought him to Canada was expected at almost any date. Then there was another ship of the same company that was going to come, and it would take him away. In spite of the representations which were made, in spite of the fact that it was pointed out time and time again that this man had no opportunity of making a proper application to come to Canada, that wherever his ship landed he would not be allowed to set foot on land legally, and therefore would be denied the facilities of making proper application, this man was eventually deported. The application to which I have already referred was submitted in Canada on August 26 by the managing director of the Victoria Tug Company. Shortly after that Nowalinski became quite seriously ill and despondent. He appeared before a medical officer, and that medical officer reported that his condition was quite serious; that he was in a very depressed state of mind and the doctor was fearful that if he was placed on board a ship and sent away he might commit suicide.
This man had a family, with one child, who were in Poland. He had never heard of them since 1949 when he left that country. He did not know whether they were alive or not. I said they were in Poland; they were in Poland if alive, but he had had no communication with them at all.
When this matter was brought to my attention, I asked the minister's department whether it would be possible to allow this man out of jail again, as his health was suffering; whether it would be possible for him to go to his friends in Victoria just for Christmas. The minister's department concurred in that suggestion. They felt it would be perfectly reasonable to allow him out of jail provided that adequate bonds were put up, and he could go to his friends to have a rest and get a decent meal at the Christmas holiday season. In fact, the department here wired their branch office in Vancouver instructing that this man should be released, but apparently that did not meet with the approval of the shipping company, which seems to have had some concern in this matter. I have a letter which was sent by Mr. E. Just Moller, operating department of the Seaboard Shipping Company Limited, to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, Vancouver, dated on Christmas eve, December 24, 1953, which reads:
Referring to your telephonic suggestion that Nowalinski should be set free because of the Christmas holidays, and considering the six-month stay in your custody, we regret that we cannot agree. The owners have instructed us to sign him on board the M.S. Nordpol, due in Seattle about January 1, 1954.
[Mr. Pearkes.l

Despite the instructions sent out from the office of the minister here in Ottawa to the officials in Vancouver the shipping company overrode those instructions. They said, this man may not go out to his friends for Christmas. It must be remembered that the only crime was of trying to escape from behind the iron curtain. However, there were people on the Pacific coast who were interested in this man's welfare and they besought the office of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in Vancouver to do something rather than to wait for the Nordpol to arrive in Vancouver.
Then an incident occurred, which was perhaps happy for the department and the shipping company. Another vessel arrived on the Pacific coast. There had been strikes and men had left the vessel because of poor conditions. This vessel has not a very savoury reputation on the Pacific coast. There was thus an opportunity for the local officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to shanghai or press-gang this unfortunate man and send him under police escort on board this vessel, the S.S. Calygera, just an hour or an hour and a half before the vessel sailed. There was no opportunity for him to get in touch with his friends to say goodbye or anything like that.
The vessel left Port Alberni and has made its way to Capetown, South Africa. This man wired from Capetown indicating that he was anxious to know whether it would be possible for him to submit an application form from Capetown for re-entry into Canada. He was told that there were no immigration facilities in Capetown and he must wait until such time as he reached some port in Europe where he would be allowed to disembark and go before the proper medical authorities and make a new and proper application for entry into Canada. Under date of February 22 the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) wrote to one of the parties who were interested in Nowalinski's welfare and he concluded with this remark:
However, as the offence against Mr. Nowalinski is solely desertion, this will not be held against him if he applies for permission to return to Canada through the proper authorities and is found able to comply with all the requirements.
If this unfortunate man is not able to get off his vessel or if his vessel does not go to a port where there are the proper facilities of the immigration department, how will it be possible for him to submit a proper application? Already an application has been made by a man who is prepared to give him employment with the Victoria Tug Company. He has been tested there and found to be a hard worker and a suitable man.

I am the last person in the world to condone any form of desertion. I realize how essential it is for the government and the immigration authorities to clamp down on seamen deserting ships and trying to make illegal entry into Canada. But surely there is a difference between a Lascar seaman trying to desert from an ordinary freighter and a refugee who is trying to find asylum after having escaped from behind the iron curtain. Surely when any responsible person in Canada, such as a director of a company, is prepared to put up bond-I have it in writing-of $50,000 for this man, or who has already put up a bond of $1,000 and guarantees him a job; surely when this man has made a proper application on the form supplied by the department endorsed by a responsible lady who is president of the Catholic Women's League of Victoria and who has a working organization behind her guaranteeing this man employment, guaranteeing him a home, prepared to take him into her own home; surely when she is supported by the clergy of his church, one of whom is an escaped Pole, I cannot help thinking that a distinction should be made between a refugee of that nature and an ordinary seaman coming to this country.
I feel that I have been justified in raising this issue at this time. I appeal to the minister to take some action in connection with this case and not to have this poor unfortunate man being shipped' from vessel to vessel and hounded all over the world without any place to go, without any opportunity of filling in the proper papers, when an application for his admission into Canada has been signed already.
I know that Mrs. Rogers is not a close relative, but this man has proved his worth.
I appeal to the minister to take some action in connection with this case and see if something cannot be done, and also to give consideration to similar cases where refugees from behind the iron curtain are seeking asylum in this country.
Hen. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration): Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief and indicate almost immediately something which probably will meet with the approval of my hon. friend. May I say without any criticism whatever that had the hon. member spoken to me before this debate commenced, or had he notified me any time in the last 24 hours that it was his intention to raise this point, we probably could have avoided this debate. I shall conclude what I have to say by reading a departmental memo which came to my hand just now after the hon. member began speaking and for which

Deportation of Polish Seaman I sent, not having had any notice up to that time that the hon. member intended to raise this point. The memo reads:
General Pearkes now inquires as to whether this man may be examined and what travel document we will accept as it is indicated this man has not been allowed to remain or land in any country. He understands-
I presume that is the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich.
-that the vessel on which he is now employed will be proceeding to the United Kingdom from South Africa.
I paraphrase the next sentence for obvious reasons, that certain inquiries are now satisfied.
When examined at Victoria, Nowalinski was in possession of a Free Poland passport issued at Dublin, Eire, on May 17, 1950, revalidated to September 4, 1951.
In order that the case may be concluded, I would recommend that the application of Mr. McGregor be accepted as meeting the requirements under section 18 (2) of the regulations and that our London office be instructed that they may grant visa on his meeting health requirements.
There follow the initials of the recording officer and a stamp on the corner "approved". I take it that that would not have to come to my attention since the department would have taken the appropriate action.
I hope that this satisfies my hon. friend. I agree he has every reason to raise this question because we are regularly confronted with the problem he has put so clearly, namely, how to distinguish between an ordinary stowaway and one who is conceivably a refugee who happens to have taken up seafaring as the only means of getting away from circumstances of which he disapproves.

I endeavoured to get in touch with the minister's office at noon and I spoke to his officials this morning, and I might mention that the papers which I asked for last January 25 were only tabled yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will be equally prompt in endeavouring to deal with a grievance which I wish to bring to his attention and to the attention of the house. I shall try to make my statement of the matter as brief as I can, but I should point out that many of us have a real grievance in that the Minister of Finance has not yet dealt with the matter about which I wish to say a word at this time.
I refer to the continuing plight of superannuated civil servants, particularly those in the lower brackets, and also to the plight of
2574	HOUSE OF
Proposed Increase in Low Superannuations the retired employees of the Canadian National Railways, especially those who are on the basic pension of only $25 a month, or little more.
It may be asked why I direct both of these matters to the attention of the Minister of Finance. I do so because it has been made clear that from the government's point of view the only way in which the government could deal with these matters is by way of putting an item in the estimates. When I have raised this matter previously during discussions on bills relating to civil service pension matters, the Minister of Finance has said that the only way to provide for an increase for superannuated civil servants in the lower brackets would be by way of an item in the estimates.
When I have raised the question of low pensions received by many C.N.R. employees it has been suggested to me that this was a matter for the C.N.R. to deal with, but as yet the C.N.R. has not taken any action, in reply to which I have pointed out that there is one small group of railway pensioners who are given some advantage by an item in the estimates. Hence both of these matters call for items to be placed in the estimates.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as everyone knows, before the end of this month the Minister of Finance, if he follows the annual practice, will be tabling supplementary estimates. We usually get that document towards the end of this month, and incidentally we are usually told that it has to be put through by the end of March.
I imagine the Minister of Finance is working on these supplementary estimates at the present time. That is the reason why I feel the matter is of sufficient urgency for me to raise it today in the hope that I can yet persuade the Minister of Finance to put two items in the supplementary estimates to cover the two groups of people to whom I have referred.
I do not wish to indulge in any form of witchcraft or fortune telling. I would not want to come under the ban of the Criminal Code in that respect. But I will go so far as to make the prediction that the Minister of Finance will not be bringing down supplementary estimates on many more occasions. In fact, since June 22 is not so far away I would not be surprised if on or about that date there might be quite a change in the life and affairs of the Minister of Finance. Perhaps it is surprising that I should pick on that particular date but it happens to be the date when the present Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada becomes 75 years


of age and I wonder whether there might not be a change involving the present Minister of Finance.
At any rate, I am sure the Minister of Finance, who has done a job which hon. members on his side of the house commend so highly, would like to tidy up some of these loose ends before he lays down this job, and I appeal to him strongly not to go out of his department leaving unfinished the problem of doing something about the pensions of these two groups of people.
With respect to the case of the superannuated civil servants, the minister knows that the figures as to their situation have been placed on the record and before the public on many occasions. I have in my hand at this moment a copy of Hansard for December 2, 1953, and I am looking at page 538 where answers are reported to questions which I asked at that time. I find that there are 325 retired civil servants drawing pensions of less than $20 a month; I find there are a total of 1,549 drawing pensions of less than $40 a month, or a total of 2,395 drawing pensions of less than $50 a month. Likewise there are 1,025 widows of retired civil servants whose pensions are less than $20 a month. There are 2,962 widows whose pensions are less than $40 a month, and there are 3,736 widows whose pensions are less than $50 a month.
As the minister knows, other jurisdictions have dealt with this problem. The government of the United Kingdom has passed bills on a number of occasions adding supplementary amounts to the pensions being received by civil servants already retired.
The United States government has done likewise. There have been at least two or three times when the position of those already retired has been improved, and when that government has recognized its responsibility to help people in view of the increase in the cost of living since they went on pension.
In this country at least two provinces, the province of Newfoundland and the province of Saskatchewan, have done something for their retired civil servants, whose pensions were in the low brackets. There are a few instances of private employers doing something along these lines. The Canadian Pacific Railway, which is not noted for its generosity in these matters, has done at least something with regard to the pensions of those in the lower brackets, between retirement and the age of 70.
As the minister knows, I believe the government should take the lead in these matters instead of always holding back and

following only what everybody else has done. However, the minister tells us, with respect to matters like this, that in his view the government should follow rather than lead. I suggest a lead has been given and that the minister should not delay any longer in dealing with this very important question.
It has been somewhat annoying to me, I may say, to have the minister tell me time and time again when I raise this question that those I am interested in have his sympathy too, that he appreciates the figures I have put forward, and so on, and that he is always prepared to give the matter consideration. But in spite of that nothing has yet been done. In the meantime, as I believe he knows, a great many representations have been made by organizations representing these people. They have been made to the minister, to other members of the government and to members in all parties and in all parts of the house.
Naturally I am in touch with a good many of these organizations, and I think it is only fair to say they have indicated to me that there have been many favourable responses from hon. members in all parts of the house. I believe that would indicate that there is wide support among the private members of this house for something being done in respect of these groups of people.
I have already given figures respecting superannuated civil servants. Similarly, Mr. Speaker, the retired employees of the Canadian National Railways include a great number whose pensions are ridiculously low. Something was done a couple of years ago by way of improving the pension plan of the Canadian National Railways. There is no doubt but that the new plan improved the position of quite a few of those who were already retired. In fact, as of March 16, 1953, according to Hansard for that date, at pages 2953 and 2954, answers to certain questions of mine showed there were 2,728 former employees who had had their pensions increased by an average amount of $17.13 a month. However, even in respect of the improvement that took place in the case of C.N.R. employees already retired, I have to point out that with regard to those whose pensions were less than $50 a month there were only 375 who got an increase, and their average increase was only $5.76 a month. On the other hand, if you go to the upper brackets you will find that those whose pensions were $150 a month or over before the change was made had an average increase of $61.23 per month. There were only 119 of those.
Proposed Increase in Low Superannuations
Similarly, it is true that those still in the service of the Canadian National Railways have had their pension plan improved even as the civil servants of Canada have had their pension position improved so far as those still in the service are concerned. But there are these two groups, the superannuated civil servants on the one hand and the retired employees of the C.N.R. on the other, who were retired some time ago when their pension benefits were much lower and for whom nothing has been done.
May I say briefly with respect to retired Canadian National employees that, according to the figures on the pages of Hansard for March 16, 1953, to which I have already referred, there are still seventeen whose pensions are less than $25 a month. There are 3,206 whose only pension from the Canadian National Railways is the basic pension of $25 a month. There is another group of 5,832 whose pensions by various combinations range between $25 and $50 a month. I might say that the cut-off point in these figures is $49.99 a month, so when you add them all together there are 9,055 retired employees of the C.N.R. whose pensions from the railway are less than $50 a month.
It is those two groups in the main, the superannuated civil servants numbering 2,395 and 3,736 widows, together with the 9,055 retired employees of the C.N.R., all of whom are receiving less than $50 a month, about whom I feel very strongly that something should be done at this time. I am not going to spend time using the kind of argument that could very well be used, the kind of argument that the man in the street is using very forcefully these days, namely that there seems to be money available for increases of other kinds and there seem to be more increases coming in addition to the ones that have already been put through at this session of parliament. There is a motion on the order paper involving a change with respect to certain other salaries from a statutory basis to a basis whereby they will be decided by the governor in council. If I know how these things work, that means an increase is coming there. I suppose the clamour in some newspaper columns for increases in the salaries of judges will probably be looked upon favourably by the government.
The man in the street sees that money seems to be available for people in much better economic circumstances than the retired pensioners to whom 1 have referred. Why is it that year after year goes by with nothing being done by the government to meet the plight of these people, as well as
2576	HOUSE OF
Proposed Increase in Low Superannuations other groups in whom I am keenly interested? As the minister and the house know, my information and my flies on these two questions are voluminous, and I could go on but I will not. The case is on the record over a number of years and I am sure, as I have already said, that there is wide support amongst private members in all sections of the house for something being done for these people. I ask the minister not to treat this just as the same old debate that the member for Winnipeg North Centre raises every once in a while, not just as something he has got to get rid of somehow, but rather as the serious question that it is.
If I am right, the minister is now in the midst of preparing the supplementary estimates which will be brought down for the end of this fiscal year, which is at the end of this month. I plead with him in the name of these two groups of people to include in the supplementary estimates the necessary items to increase these pensions, particularly for those in the lower brackets. Let there be no further delay.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: C.N.R. PENSIONERS
speechtext: And as generous?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: C.N.R. PENSIONERS
speechtext:
I think I can do so because I have had to deal with this question on a number of other occasions. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is of course not the only member of the house who is interested in the matter. A great many members are interested in it. I have received representations from many on both sides of the house. He has cited before the figures he cited this year as to the number of pensioners under the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Canadian National pension plan who are in receipt of relatively small pensions.
I am not too familiar with the Canadian National pension plan because of course that is primarily the responsibility of the management of the Canadian National Railways. But I am familiar with the civil service superannuation plan because I am responsible for introducing such amendments to that plan as are made from time to time. It means very little for my hon. friend to quote figures as to the size of these pensions without indicating the length of service of the pensioner.
(Mr. Knowles.]

In point of fact, the civil service superannuation plan is probably the most generous pension plan in Canada. It is certainly one of the most generous and one of the most favourable for the pensioner. It is quite a bit more favourable than the pension plan of the Canadian Pacific Railway, to which the hon. member alluded, and in which I understand some adjustments were made.
It means very little to cite figures of pensioners who are in receipt of pensions of $15 to $20 a month. They may only have been, and probably were, in the government service a comparatively short time. One must assume that while they were employed in other walks of life they were or should have been, in common with hundreds of thousands of other Canadian citizens, making some provision for their own pension needs. I have always felt that the position of the civil service pensioner was no different from that of any other Canadian citizen who may not be eligible for a pension plan, who may not be working for a company which has a pension plan in force or is self-employed and is required to furnish his own pension either by buying annuity policies, by buying a government annuity, by investing in bonds, or by any other form of investment which he believes will make the best provision for his later years.
Since the recipients under pension provisions of that kind have no means of getting an automatic increase in their pensions because of the effect of inflation or any other cause, I have never felt that those who are in receipt of pensions provided by taxpayers who are putting up the money for them should be in a better position than those taxpayers themselves. It is for that reason I have consistently said in the house I felt there was not a case for treating civil service pensioners in any different way than the holder of any other contractual obligation. I still hold that view. Under those circumstances, I think my hon. friend will appreciate that I have no intention of recommending the inclusion in the supplementary estimates of an item to provide for an increase in those pensions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: And the Liberals applaud that statement.

Notwithstanding the reasons which the minister has given, I feel that the members of this house and the government ought to give most serious consideration to the plight of all those who now find themselves unable to live upon the incomes which they are receiving, and who are unable to increase those incomes

by any means available to them. I feel that we cannot possibly escape that responsibility. In a country that is producing $24 billion worth of goods a year, there can be no conceivable excuse for permitting anyone to suffer from the lack of the necessities of life.
While I am dealing with that question, in respect of which I support the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I wish to direct attention once more to the intolerable plight of our senior citizens. The cost of living has so increased that our senior citizens are again the victims of slow starvation. This is a matter not to be tolerated at all by the people of Canada, and particularly by the members of parliament in this dominion.

speechtext:
Perhaps I might say just one word to repeat the understanding which I think we reached about the manner in which this particular item would be dealt with. I think it was understood that the item being called covered the construction of the national film board building in Montreal. Of course, it covers as well all the other matters in the province of Quebec, but it was agreed that we would confine discussion at first to the business of the national film board building and when that was completed we would
Supply-National Film Board carry the item after other discussion that there might be on that particular item. We would then revert to the item covering general administration of public works.
The national film board, as hon. members know, Mr. Chairman, has been confined to nine or ten buildings in the city of Ottawa since its inception, and under those conditions have done what I consider an excellent job on behalf of the public of Canada in the production and distribution of film. The film board has twice been reconstituted, so to speak, that is, a revision of its statute and its activities, the last one being in 1950, and there was a parliamentary committee of this house in 1952.
The decision which has been made to build the buildings to house the activities of the board in the city of Montreal or Ville St. Laurent, as it is more properly known, dates back at least two years and was communicated both to the committee, as I recall it, and to the house. The references were set out in certain remarks made by the Prime Minister, and referred to by the Leader of the Opposition earlier in this session, and will be given in more detail as the debate proceeds, if there is a debate. The real purpose, however, of building at this moment is to house in one building the activities of the board because of the manifest inefficiency which now exists through having to conduct their operations in nine or ten places. It is accompanied as well by a policy decision that the national film board, generally speaking, with its present activities, is a continuing need in this country, and one which this government should maintain.
I quite realize that there has been at various times criticism of the film board and its activities. But, as happens in so many cases, that criticism is in our opinion more than offset by the support given to the board by the many public bodies, and by the obvious demand for the product they turn out.
The board therefore presented to us over the past three or four years urgent requests for the construction of a suitable building. Now, before it was decided to accede to these requests it was passed upon, first by the Massey commission, and secondly by J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited. And I might interject here that I did not suggest in the statement I made earlier in this session that the J. D. Woods and Gordon report recommended a site in the city of Montreal. If any such impression was gained from what I said it was unintentional on my part. It was

Supply-National Film Board merely that they recommended a building, and the government accepted that decision.
I have noticed in the press that the building itself has been described in various terms, very few of which have any semblance of reality. It is quite true that the contract price was $5,250,000, and that is a considerable sum of money to spend at any time. But the building now contains only those items which in the opinion of the board are essential for the proper functioning of their activities.
There may be marble walls, as I have heard it reported. If so, then they are very limited, in the entrance hall itself. No luxury of that type is being indulged in, in any way. However, the equipment of the building, the essential equipment, which now is not owned by the board, and which they feel is necessary for a proper carrying out of their duties, as laid down by them, is the establishing of a stage from which they can take acting films for use in their work. They now have to rent similar facilities, and in fact do from time to time rent those facilities from others.
It is true that there is in the building a small auditorium, one which is to be used of course for the viewing of films as they are being produced, as they are being cut, and so on. The committee will understand that the production of films is an expensive process. One does not do this without the expenditure of some money. Indeed, I believe the estimates contain an item in the order of $3,200,000 this year for the national film board. This sum is expended in the production of approximately four hundred films of one kind or another, including newsreels, feature length films, so called, dub-ins, and other types of films.
For that reason, and after careful consideration of the facilities available in private industry, and recognizing that the government's position in respect of the board has always been that it is providing certain results which could not be provided otherwise, and after a review to see if that is still the case, the government concluded that it was, and thought we should vote this sum of money for the purpose of providing a building for the film board.
I do not propose to develop anything further at the moment by way of justification for the expenditure. The details of the building are of course more properly within the knowledge and competence of description of the Minister of Public Works. To some extent my remarks may have been out of order, except for the belief on our part, when we discussed this matter the other day, that it would not be possible, Mr. Chairman, to

confine the debate wholly to the actual building itself, since no doubt hon. members would like to discuss whether or not any building is needed.
However, the details of that building, its probable cost and the information as to its value, can be discussed by the Minister of Public Works, who is not only now in the position of having the terms of the contract before him but as well in my opinion, as I said before, is responsible for the present efficient management of the national film board and has brought it to the point where I think it is discharging in excellent fashion the duties laid upon it by parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the time of the committee to say something about this item. May I preface my remarks with the statement that in a general way I approve of the work of the national film board. I think it is very good, and has been well conducted. As a matter of fact I have wondered at times how they have been able to carry on as well as they have in the quarters in which they were housed.
My concern with the matter arises from the one point of moving the site of the film board from Ottawa to another city, another part of the country. Unfortunately, perhaps I am guilty, along with other hon. members, of not realizing earlier that this move was imminent. As a matter of fact, it may not be possible to excuse oneself on that score; but whether we can or cannot, we are confronted now with a situation in which a contract has been let for the construction of a building in Montreal for the film board.
My request today is for a withholding of the actual work under that contract until some matters of policy are discussed and settled, and the announcement concerning them is made.
I think perhaps it would be of interest when discussing this matter to look at the National Film Act, itself. If one reads the headnotes in the act he will find that the purposes of the board are set out in section 9. Perhaps it would be helpful if I were to place it on record. Section 9 is as follows:
The board is established to initiate and promote the production and distribution of films in the national interest and in particular
(a)	to produce and distribute and to promote the production and distribution of films designed to interpret Canada to Canadians and to other nations:
(b)	to represent the government of Canada in its relations with persons engaged in commercial motion picture film activity in connection with motion picture films for the government or any department thereof;
(c)	to engage in research in film activity and to make available the results thereof to persons engaged in the production of films;

(d)	to advise the governor in council in connection with film activities; and
(e)	to discharge such other duties relating to film activities as the governor in council may direct it to undertake.
In addition to these purposes of the film board, subsection 1 of section 11 has a direct bearing, and it reads:
(1) Kxcept with the approval of the governor in council, no department shall initiate the production or processing of a motion picture film without the authority of the board, and the production and processing of all motion picture films by or for departments shall be undertaken by the board unless the board is of opinion that it is in the public interest that it be otherwise undertaken and authorizes it to be so undertaken.
In other words, if the two sections are read together, it becomes clear that the function of the board is primarily directed to advising the government on the production of films for government use, and it is contemplated of course that such films will not be produced otherwise than by the film board, without their concurrence.
The situation as I see it is this. The work of the film board has increased from year to year, and in the main it has been very good work, until last year when the number of films produced was of the order of 400. This is certainly an increase in work and involves some new departures. Of that number of 400 films, I have not the precise details as to how many were made for government departments or directly in connection with the work of government and how many originated with the film board itself. That raises two or three new questions, questions that never existed in the early work of the film board because of the nature of its work.
The first question is that of censorship. It is, I would think, obvious that in the field of film production, other than films produced for government departments in connection with work that comes within the orbit of federal authority under the British North America Act, the films are subject to provincial censorship. Before we embark on the erection of this building I should like to see some clarification of whether or not the government is going to be able to continue in that new field of production of films. If it is, what is the relationship with the provincial authorities in the field of censorship? That is a new problem or matter of policy that has to be settled with respect to the film board, and that did not arise or exist to any appreciable extent four years ago when the first preliminary steps were taken to acquire a site in Montreal for a new plant. That problem of course exists whether the film board is located in Ontario, Quebec or anywhere else. It is a problem that is going to affect the
Supply-National Film Board size of operation, and therefore in my view is a problem that will have to be dealt with as a preliminary to the construction of any building wherever located.

Will the hon. member
permit a question? What does he as a lawyer think of the authority or jurisdiction of a provincial government with respect to censorship of films of an organization of the federal government?

I would think they have no right at all of censorship of those films that have to do with other government activities that clearly are within the federal jurisdiction. Let me answer the hon. member for Prince Albert by taking an example. Assume that we are dealing with a film having to do with the work of the Department of Agriculture, or that part of it that is clearly within federal jurisdiction. I would think that such films would not be subject to censorship by the provinces. It is when you get into this other class of film that is not directly related to federal government activity that the difficulty arises. There is a whole field there that requires clarification, and I think that clarification should come before a building is constructed. Anyway, it is going to make a big difference whether the film board is operating on the scale of production of 400, 500 or 600 films a year or is back to the scale of 100 or 200 films a year, and that also applies to the type of building required.
As far as the building itself is concerned, judging from any information I have about the particular building, it is perfectly satisfactory to me. I have no objections to the type of building or anything related to it; but there is another matter that arises. It is claimed by some persons and by some national organizations that the government should go out of the film production business altogether, and that it should be returned to private enterprise. I for one do not subscribe to that view. To begin with, I do not think it would be possible to do so, even if the government so desired, because the private film industry in Canada could not undertake that work. Even if it were desirable, the private film industry is not sufficiently developed to undertake it.
There should be some determination as to what pattern is going to be followed with respect to the use of the private film industry in the production of film board films for the federal government. As far as I am aware, we have been given no statement of policy in that connection, and I would suggest that matter must be settled here by the govern-

Supply-National Film Board ment before we can determine whether or not we should proceed with this building.
As I say, I do not subscribe to the view that the film production for the government should be returned to private industry; but certainly I do subscribe to the view that that whole question is of such a nature that it must be examined, and the question of policy determined as to what type of production should go to private industry and to what extent it is possible for private industry to handle it.
There is another matter that bothers me about this move. The work of the film board is such that it is not easy for this house to examine its expenditures. This type of work is such that there is no easy formula that one can apply to determine whether they are using their money expenditures efficiently or not. No one can give me any formula that would be of much use in that connection. I raise that for this reason. It is going to be a continuing government expenditure on a larger scale, I would think, as the years go by. My view is that it is desirable that such an activity of government should be under the control of government where it can be very easily watched, not only by hon. members, but by the ministers concerned.
In that connection it is rather interesting to notice the activities of government that have been started in other cities and brought back to Ottawa in the last few years. I can refer to two of them. One was Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. This corporation by its nature carried on operations very much like a commercial business and it was decided to bring the administrative head office to Ottawa from Toronto. Then there was another activity of the government which was purely commercial. I refer to the disposal of surplus war materials by War Assets Corporation. This corporation was moved to Ottawa from Montreal.
If it was thought necessary or desirable in controlling these types of commercial activity to bring these companies back to Ottawa, I suggest respectfully that it is just that much more desirable that the activities of the film board be kept here. But there is another thing. The nature of the work of the film board is such that I do not think it is proper to describe it as a commercial activity. As a matter of fact I have not found any adequate way to describe it.
The work of the film board has to do with the interpreting of Canada to Canadians and to other nations. That is found in the


first subsection of the act defining the purposes of the board. It has to do with the expression of the cultural aspirations of the Canadian people in a collective way. When you get to a matter of that sort it becomes a question of some delicacy. You are dealing with the medium of expression of the culture of the Canadian people, one part of the country to another and the whole of the country to other parts of the world.
Perhaps it would be well for us in committee today to recall the struggle in the development of the nationhood of this country. At the time of the Act of Union, and after, there was a struggle to find some common ground where there could be a meeting together of the people in the capital of their country. We recall the long history of the period when the capital was in Toronto, in Kingston, in Montreal, in Quebec and in Hamilton at one point. There was constant trouble, a constant feeling of division, constant dissatisfaction.
Ottawa was later chosen as the capital of the country. I am not one who asserts that that is wholly satisfactory to all Canadians, but I do suggest respectfully that that choice has made possible the development of a feeling of Canadianism to a very great degree. Canadian citizens generally have come to look on this choice of the site of their capital, on the river at the boundaries of the two older provinces, as being a satisfactory one, as being one which they felt they could accept fully.
I venture the opinion now that if you were to go among those little groups-I believe they are called film societies- throughout the rural sections of this country and ask them about this move and discuss it, you would find they all felt that Ottawa was and should be the location of any centre that was to express their national culture, any centre that was to typify the expression of their national culture and they would want a medium such as this film board kept in their capital city and not sent to any other part of the country. It is here that they feel they can unite in that feeling and not elsewhere in the country, however attractive and desirable other parts of the country would be to any one of them.
I am one who has a rather strong feeling, which I think is shared by other hon. members in this house, about the rapid development of the sense of Canadian citizenship. This has gone on at a tremendously accelerated pace during the last fifteen years. I would hate to see anything done that would

tend to separate any of us from that feeling and from the feeling that in our capital we have achieved a centre where that feeling can find its expression.
There is a danger in an activity like this, where you are dealing with the creative arts and the cultural feelings of the people, in moving it away, that you will lose something of value in the expressing and fostering and developing of a feeling of Canadian citizenship.
There are perhaps other things that could be said. It may be unfortunate that this move became a reality when parliament was not sitting. That cannot be helped, as it was in the ordinary course of events; but it is unfortunate in that much misinformation was spread about. Many things were said which in my view ought not to have been said. They were not accurate and did not deal with the merits of the suggested change of site.
By the way as far as the actual site chosen in Montreal is concerned, I have no quarrel with it. I think probably the Department of Public Works showed shrewd judgment of land values when they acquired the site they did. I am told that the site is quite a valuable piece of property. As far as I am concerned, I have no criticism to offer in that regard.
My criticism centres on the one point. I do not think sufficient preliminary matters were decided to warrant any decision as to whether or not the film board should be moved. It may well be that after these other matters are considered and decided the film board ought to be moved out of Ottawa; but I for one cannot see the possibility of that, although, as I say, it may well be so.
My view is that even at this late date the government should consider these other matters of policy in relation to the whole operation of the board and have those matters of policy announced and dealt with before this building is proceeded with. I know it is possible to say with correctness that an item covering the acquisition of the land appeared in the estimates some years ago. I know we can all be criticized somewhat for not sharply taking issue at that point. My own view was that I did not think the move was imminent, and I think if I checked Hansard I could show justification for taking that view. In any event, whether or not that is the case, I suggest it is irrelevant.
The contractor dealing with this particular contract is perfectly reputable, and I would respectfully ask the government to withhold the work, at the risk of having to pay some 83276-164
Supply-National Film Board damages to the contractor until these other matters affecting the wisdom of moving the national film board away from the capital city are determined and settled.

Mr. Chairman, I deferred my remarks in regard to this subject, which I have raised on a number of occasions, because I thought the Minister of Public Works might be supplementing the remarks already made by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
However, I assume from the fact that he has not done so that he leaves the matter where it rests with the statement given to us by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
A great deal more is involved in the discussion of this item than the authority of the film board, the policies to be followed in the production of future films, the type of building to be erected, the location or any of the other subjects which have been raised. The most important issue before this house at the moment is the responsibility of parliament itself.
It has been said that one of the unfortunate facts was that this decision had not been reached when parliament was sitting. But it was. A decision was reached while we were sitting here. A decision was reached within the past few weeks, after we had been assured by the Prime Minister that a decision would not be reached until the house had had an opportunity to consider this item. For that reason there should be no hesitation on the part of the government in announcing without any reservation that this contract will stand, and will not be proceeded with until the house has the information which has never been presented to it, and until members of parliament have an opportunity to express some opinion in regard to the information which is not yet available.
The wisdom of erecting a building in Ottawa, in Ville St. Laurent or at any other point in Canada, is not the primary issue under discussion. The fact is that no member of this parliament, except perhaps the Minister of Public Works, has yet before him or her any information upon which to pass judgment. If the Minister of Public Works has such information, then it is a well guarded secret.
This is not parliamentary procedure. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has reviewed certain features of this subject with which I would like to deal briefly. I wish to refer to them because I do want to dispose

Supply-National Film. Board of some of the suggestions which have been made as to the point of view from which this subject is being approached.
The minister has said that the film board has been doing an excellent job. I have heard no suggestion to the contrary. It happens that I am one of the many enthusiasts who have for some time followed the hobby of both taking and showing moving picture films. I have shown many films produced by the national film board on a projector which has given me a great deal of pleasure in my own house. I can speak with some measure of personal experience about the films produced by the film board, and I am in a position to compare them because the projector I own happens to be able to handle either sound or stills, and I have shown films produced in different parts of the world as well as in different parts of this continent.
The films which I have shown, and which others have seen with pleasure, are excellent productions. I mention that only to remove right away from consideration in this discussion any suggestion that the views I may put forward relate to the quality of the production.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration also referred to the suggestion that the board should discontinue the production of films. Let me dispose of that at the outset. I have never made that suggestion. I am convinced that there are many fields of specialized production in which it is essential that we have films produced under the supervision of a government agency. I am not sure that remark applies to many of the films that are being produced, in spite of the generally excellent quality of most of the films.
There are two fields where it is of special service to the country and to our people to have productions of this kind available, namely, in the field of education and in the field of national defence. There is an old Chinese maxim that one picture tells more than ten thousand words. I am convinced that we have not yet even touched the possibility of the moving picture with sound for educational purposes.
I have seen films used for educational purposes in a way which convinces me that we could extend their use far beyond anything that has yet been attempted. For example, take the teaching of a subject such as physics. It would be possible to show the operations of an internal combustion engine, a jet engine, or anything of that kind in a cut model where the operation could be simplified by slow motion photography in a way that would not


have been possible with any model which could readily become available in any physics classroom in this country.
It is possible to teach history by means of the moving picture film in a way that cannot easily be approached in the junior classes by any textbook, no matter how readable or how well illustrated it may be. It is possible to use film for teaching languages in a way that we have not employed it, to show not only the way in which the sounds are formed but certain well-recognized principles with regard to the projection of the human voice and the actual use of words themselves in a manner that is more interesting to the pupil when those words come from someone whose name is well known to him. When the living history of this time can be portrayed in the classroom in the words of men like Churchill, Roosevelt and others of the present and recent generation, we can see the possibilities of attracting our young people to the use of language in a way that has not yet been possible.
In the teaching of language in this country film would be of immense value. We still have a long way to go in teaching French in the English-speaking parts of Canada and in teaching English in the French-speaking parts of Canada. This is one of the aids that can come to the help of teachers and which can be of great value in that field. I can see there a great public service in the production of films of a type that possibly could not be produced satisfactorily on a strictly commercial basis.
Then there is the question of national defence. We learned how much importance the government attaches to films produced for national defence purposes when we were informed within the last two years of the suspension of the activities of the national film board in producing films for national defence purposes because of the uncertainty of the government about some security risks within the board. Whether that was a wise or unwise decision is still unknown to members on this side of the house because we only have the statement of the government as to the course it followed. Nevertheless this did place dramatic emphasis upon the importance the government attaches to films produced for national defence purposes.
There again we have not even started to explore the possibilities of instruction by films of this kind. We have produced a number of films. We could go far beyond anything that has yet been attempted, with great economy in the money devoted to teaching because of the amount that would be saved through placing this medium of instruction in the

hands of members of the units themselves who could give instruction with films of this kind.
In the Royal Canadian Air Force, the artillery, the infantry, the tank corps, the armoured forces, the medical services, the engineers, in the navy with all its new ramifications of defensive as well as offensive equipment, in every branch of the services, there is a tremendous field scarcely yet explored. All this imposes certain conditions before a decision can be reached as to what should be done.
When we come to the matter of censorship, which was mentioned, surely there can be no question but that censorship would apply with equal force to films produced by the dominion government as to those produced by any other agency. I cannot believe for a moment that the suggestion would be made that censorship could be circumvented in the showing of films in any theatre simply by virtue of the fact that they were produced by an agency of the dominion government.
That was not my suggestion.

I was about to say that I felt sure that was not the suggestion. Nevertheless that could become a very real question if the activities were extended to a point where a considerable number of films produced by the national film board were being shown in those places where provincial censorship would ordinarily apply. This makes it obvious that here is another consideration which needs to be resolved before a final decision can be made as to what should be done with regard to this subject.
I have put these matters forward merely to indicate how many things there are that we should know before any single member of the house is in a position to say that $1 million, $5 million, $10 million or $1 should be expended. Surely if we are to justify the high estimate of the responsibility of members which has been asserted on a number of occasions within the past few weeks we should exhibit it on this occasion, when this matter comes before us for the very first time. When it comes before us, may I repeat, for the very first time, when this is the first opportunity that has been presented to discuss the question with knowledge of the facts, every one of us should insist that we know what are the facts upon which this decision has been made, that we know what is the authority of the film board, and that we know what is now the stated policy of the government with respect to the production of films in this building when it is constructed.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration said the real purpose in constructing this

He then went on to say that a decision of policy was involved, in that there was to be a continued operation of this board. Mr. Chairman, it involves a great deal more than that. It involves a decision of policy by the government not only that there is to be continued operation of the film board but also involves, surely, a decision of policy as to what the scope of the activities of the film board will be and the nature of the production, with respect to which the government made a decision without consulting parliament as to the location of the building.
It may well be that there are many good and sound reasons for selecting the site that has been chosen. If there are, then let us have them. If there are, then let us all agree that if we are to accept our responsibilities as members of parliament in deciding on this item we must know these reasons before we approve an item that carries with it this major decision.
It involves also some understanding of the alance of consideration, remembering that neither the Massey commission, the group of experts known as J. D. Woods and Gordon nor the national film board committee of this house that reported in 1952 made any suggestion that there should be a change in the location of the building. Therefore we must go entirely outside of the evidence before the Massey commission and the decisions of the Massey commission; we must go entirely beyond the report of J. D. Woods and Gordon-we must go beyond the report of the national fihn board committee of this house in 1952, to find the reason for this decision.
It was stated in the proceedings of that committee.

It is clear in the proceedings.

We must have some other evidence if we are to reach a decision which even remotely suggests that we are accepting our responsibilities as members of this house.
Nor is it alone the location of this building which is of great importance. Exactly what type of building is required? In order

Supply-National Film Board to form any judgment on that part we must know what the policy is concerning the scope of activities, the expected production and the expected employment level of the national film board. There are some other considerations about which we should know. Today, as anyone with the slightest knowledge of film production is well aware, there is no operation more sensitive to sound. Even the technical handling of television is not so dependent upon the elimination of extraneous sound, because any sound reaching the recording equipment during film production will be permanently recorded.
Let no one suggest that we are in a position to pass judgment as to whether or not that has been dealt with. We have not had a word on this subject from the government as yet. In deciding where a national film board building is to be established we certainly should be told what consideration has been given to the sound factors, particularly having regard to the well known impact on film of the highly reproductive, high-pitched screech of a jet motor. This is another question about which we should have some information, and the government has not told us anything about it.
At this time it must be quite clear that we should have a statement of the terms of reference under which the film board is to operate, and the instructions the film board has received as to the scope of its activities, A question has been raised already as to the need for a statement of policy as to whether production is to be in the nature of 100, 400 or 500 films. This would be determined by the field of activity contemplated by the government. What we need, and need greatly, if there is to be an understanding of this problem is a clarification of the government's decision concerning the real function of the national film board.
The truth is, and I do not think for one moment any member of the government would deny it, that this board has grown up like Topsy. Probably in many cases the person who was most surprised by the nature of the activities of the film board was the minister who was responsible for that board. Every now and then the minister would see a film and say, "Well, this is better than I thought." On another occasion the minister might say, with some measure of surprise, he had not known the field was covered to that extent.
To which minister are you referring?
I hope it would include most of the ministers, but I am certain it applies to the present Minister of Public Works.
I just wanted to know which ones.
I shall be quite prepared to let my remarks apply to the minister now responsible.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You would not want me to make the obvious retort?

If my hon. friend means that the minister who spoke on behalf of the Minister of Public Works is in the same position, I certainly would think that is the obvious retort, because I am quite sure the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was greatly surprised at some of the films that he found had actually been produced. Perhaps he shared with some of the rest of us a great measure of satisfaction, surprised satisfaction on some occasions, as to the nature of the films that were produced. None of us received any information in this house to give us the slightest idea of what films were being produced, beyond the general statements that were made.
When I say that, I recognize that there is an excellent index of the films produced by the film board. I do not expect I will hear from either the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration or any other minister that they have seen all these films. I have not, and I do not think any of the other hon. members have. It would take a very long time to see them all. I am not suggesting the ministers have a duty to do that. I do suggest, however, there should be some procedure by which there would be supervision of the films produced within such terms of reference and such declarations of policy as may be announced to this house for the first time by this government. I say "for the first time", because any declaration of policy in the past has been in such general terms that it never defined the real scope of the activities of this board.
Now I want to point out why it is so necessary that we get complete information in this occasion. The subject matter was discussed earlier this year, and is recorded in Hansard of January 19. I shall again place on the record what was said on that occasion, so that it may be contained in the context of the remarks I make at this time. I asked the Prime Minister this question:
I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Can the Prime Minister say whether press reports appearing during the last twenty-four hours respecting the national film hoard are correct and if the

government does intend to reconsider its decision to move the national film board from Ottawa? At the same time I would ask whether there will be an opportunity to discuss the matter if this is so.
To this the Prime Minister replied:
There has been no decision reached in that matter.
That was on January 19.
Of this year?

Yes, January 19, 1954. The
Prime Minister said:
There has been no decision reached in that matter. What is under consideration at the present time is the tenders that were submitted for the construction of a building in Montreal. They are all of a very substantial amount, and the matter that is now under consideration is as to whether or not the government will recommend the appropriations required for that large expenditure at this time.
Then I said:
Do I understand from what the Prime Minister has said that, having regard to the amount involved, the government may actually be reconsidering whether it will or will not move the national film board from Ottawa?
To that the Prime Minister replied:
No decision has been reached in that regard, but until the government comes to parliament with a definite recommendation for a definite amount to be expended for a building at a definite place there is always a possibility that changes in the recommendation may be made.
Now, it is upon that completely unqualified assurance by the Prime Minister that I base my request-I shall go further; that I base my demand, and a justified demand-that the Minister of Public Works state unequivocally that everything will be suspended in relation to this contract until parliament has heard the reasons, and until there has been an opportunity to consider those reasons.

speechtext: Well-

The minister will have plenty of chance to deal with this matter. Let me read what happened on the following day, as recorded in Hansard for January 20, upon which occasion I raised a question of privilege:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege in relation to a statement made to the house yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). Yesterday afternoon, in response to a question, the Prime Minister made the statement that the question of the removal of the national film board remained an open one until some definite item would be brought before the house.
And may I interject here that if the Prime Minister had any question about the accuracy of the statement I have just referred to, that was the time for him to state it. Then I continued:
Then in the late afternoon edition of the Ottawa Journal I read that the definite recommendation in regard to the adoption of a tender for the construction of the national film board building was definitely going to the treasury board. It seems to me that these statements are inconsistent. Having regard to the general principle involved and the assurance by the Prime Minister that we would have something before us before this move was definite, it seems to me that we should know what the situation is.
To that the Prime Minister replied, not that there had been no assurance, but rather that he hoped the house would rely upon his statement instead of a press statement. This is what he said:
Mr. Speaker, I would hope that the house would take the statements made by the government in the house in preference to speculative reports by newspapers.
The fact is that those words are clear and unequivocal; they are clear and understandable; they are clear and definite. It was quite certain from those words that every member in the house who heard them had a right to expect that we would have this item before us before any decision was made in regard to those tenders.

Nevertheless it turned out that, contrary to the information received from the Prime Minister, the subject was under consideration and a decision was made by the government to proceed with tenders. The tender was awarded to a company in Toronto. This company has been given the contract to go to Montreal and construct this building there.
That also is something about which I would like to have information before this item is disposed of. I want to know who the contractors were who bid, the amount of the tenders, the bond that has been called for, and the previous experience in a specialized line of construction of this type that was insisted upon in calling for tenders. After all, these buildings are very intricate. They are buildings of a highly technical type, and I want to know the extent to which assurance was secured that the tenders were upon a basis that left no doubt that the tenderer was highly qualified in this particular and unusual field of construction.
