speakeroldname: Mrs. Ellen L. Fairclough (Hamilton West) moved
subtopic: MEASURE TO REQUIRE EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 2, to provide equal pay for equal work for women.
She said: Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to have the opportunity of presenting this legislation for the consideration of parliament. This is a measure to prevent discrimination against women in respect of their employment by reason of their sex and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, to ensure that women will be paid at the same rates as men for similar or comparable work.
There are many points which might be enumerated as one studies more and more the ramifications of this type of legislation. Since world war I the use of women in industry and commerce, in many instances in so-called men's jobs, has become more and more commonplace. In the factory, in the office, in the school and in the home women are performing work of a comparable character to that performed by men. Where it was thought at one time that the utilization of women in the labour force was a matter of passing interest it has now become apparent that they are needed in a rapidly expanding economy. As working conditions have improved for all workers the classifications which were regarded as strictly male have gradually diminished in number. This is true in industry, and I suppose it is far truer in clerical, executive and professional jobs.
The principle of equal pay for equal work is one which has been espoused by trade unions, industrial organizations and the like for many years, but there are a great many workers in all lines of activity who do not
2590	HOUSE OF
Industrial Status of Women enjoy the protection .or bargaining advantages of union membership. It is partly because of these workers that it is advisable to have legislation enacted by the government under whose jurisdiction they come.
Three years ago such legislation was enacted in Ontario. Last year Saskatchewan brought a similar law into effect. British Columbia adopted equal pay legislation last year, which came into force on January 1 of this year. Provincial laws cover most of the workers of this country, but there are still a number of employees who because of the nature of their employment or the districts in which they reside come under federal jurisdiction. It is to cover those workers that I have introduced this bill.
I might say that a great deal of the opposition which formerly greeted such legislation has disappeared in the light of increasing knowledge that such legislation benefits men as well as women. Some of the main points which must be considered are that women represent the nation's greatest labour reserve. It is from their ranks that additional workers must be drawn in the event of the need for the rapid acceleration of defence production, for instance. This type of legislation would facilitate their recruitment.
From the standpoint of the women themselves, it is a matter of simple justice. It ensures that women workers will receive what they are entitled to receive for the work they do. Those women who are housewives and mothers also have an interest in this type of legislation because it protects them and their children in that it protects the wages of their husbands.
Equal pay affords to men greater wage and job security. It protects them from the exploitation of employers who would hire women for less money or who would replace men workers with women workers at lower rates.
Equal pay legislation is also a protection to the employers, who are thus protected from the unfair competition of those who would attempt to use women to undercut men's wages. Studies which have been made on this subject are great in number and voluminous in character. I have here a publication of the department of labour in the United States which came out recently. The introduction states in part:
Women's present status provides freedom to participate in a broad range of activities almost unknown to the woman of fifty years ago. The import of this freedom can be fully understood only by realizing that its foundations rest not alone in the vast achievements of the movement for women's rights, but in the complexities of a changing social and economic order with its revolutionizing effects upon home and work life.


It is true that the last 50 years have seen many changes. There has been a decided trend toward what you might call urbanization. As the urban sections of our land have grown in size, living accommodation has become more and more restricted. Several families now occupy the space formerly occupied by one family. This has had its effect on domestic staffs. It is very hard to say which came first, the chicken or the egg, whether the lack of domestic help during the period of the first world war forced people with large homes to cut down the space they occupied and thus make it easier for the woman of the house to handle her own housework, or whether the women themselves, wishing to be free of the extra responsibility of large homes and the management of domestic staffs, purposely cut down on those staffs which then were left free to find their way into other than domestic work. Whatever the cause, certainly a great change has taken place in the last 50 years.
Women were released more and more from the domestic responsibilities which were at one time accepted as their main work, and found their way into many types of activity. They went into organizational work, into church work, into club work, into patriotic, religious and social work. As they became more and more interested in these organizations they also became more and more interested in the world which lay outside their own homes. I think the great interest which is taken today by parents generally in associations connected with education is proof of the extent to which women have found that a participation in community affairs has a direct effect upon their own manner of living and upon the advantages which are made available not only to them but to their children.
Be that as it may, it is true that as time went on women who had more freedom, who had more time on their hands, gradually found their way into both industrial and commercial work. There is no doubt at all that this situation came about largely due to the demands which were made upon them in the two world wars through which we have come in the last 50 years; but having once taken their place in the industrial, commercial, and professional life of this country they were loath to relinquish that place, and indeed industry, commerce, and the professions were loath to see them go back to their homes and leave the positions which they had filled with such efficiency and poise all those years.

I recall young women whom I knew during the last world war who were doing jobs which formerly would have been completely foreign to a woman. For example, I remember a couple of young women I knew who were operating huge cranes in the steel plant in Hamilton, and certainly that is the type of work which at one time would have been thought to be entirely within the field of male employment. Nevertheless they did that job and did it well. It is true, as this book states:
They have indeed been both "pushed" and "pulled" out of an area of activity once circumscribed by the household-"pushed" by the lesser requirements upon their time and interest by the withdrawal from the home of many productive activities, and "pulled" by expanding opportunities and the demands for income in an economy of ever-increasing living standards.
I believe it is true to say, Mr. Speaker, that as living standards have progressed the desire of all homemakers has been for an even higher standard of living which could not be attained on the wages of one single worker in the home. It is true, as this book goes on to say, that both men and women are victims of tradition and prejudice, and both are affected by what Mildred Thompson, until recently dean of Vassar College, describes as a "mode of thinking which has not caught up with the actual conditions of our times."
The basic reason for this legislation, Mr. Speaker, is not to protect the woman who is a rare case. It is not to make sure that some individual or group of individuals shall benefit under this legislation. Rather it is simply to protect the great rank and file of women workers, many of whom have no bargaining agents, who have no one to speak for them and to produce and maintain a bargaining procedure through which they can obtain the advantages they desire, and also abolish the discrimination under which they work at the present time.
Recent years have witnessed a rapid growth in employment. The latest census figures show that as of October 24, 1953, the labour force numbered 5,357,000 of which 4,166,000 or 77-8 per cent were men and 1,185,000 or 22-2 per cent were women. The figure has been running at around 23 per cent of the labour force for a number of years. As a matter of fact in 1949 it was 23-5 per cent, and according to the monthly bulletin of employment and payrolls the latest figures for December, 1953, show an increase from November to December of from 222 per thousand to 227 per thousand, which brings it back to about the 23 per cent figure.
Of those women who were thus gainfully employed well over half have made their 83276-165i
Industrial Status of Women income tax returns for the year 1950 and, according to the taxation statistics for 1952, practically half a million of them were single with no dependents, about 24,000 were married with no dependents, and about 27,500 both single and married had to support dependents ranging from one to five. It is interesting to note that some of these women have been supporting more than five dependents. This substantial number of people represents quite a considerable portion of the labour force of this country, many of whom have been suffering discrimination by reason of a wage differential from the beginning of time.
I think at this stage we might well have a look at the history of equal remuneration legislation in many other parts of the world. As long ago as 1919 the constitution of the international labour organization proclaimed the "special and urgent importance" of "the principle that men and women should receive equal remuneration for work of equal value." That principle was enunciated in article 41. Then in 1948 when the constitution of ILO was amended the preamble proclaimed that "improvement (of conditions of labour) is urgently required by recognition of the principle of equal remuneration for work of equal value."
The first country to establish the principle of equal pay by constitutional provisions was Mexico in 1917; and since that time, according to the report of the committee of the thirty-third session of the international labour conference-which was the last report containing this information-16 other countries have adopted equal pay legislation. In addition, two states in Germany have also adopted it.
In the United States of America 13 states and the territory of Alaska have enacted equal pay laws. In Canada, as I previously mentioned, three provinces have adopted equal pay legislation. It was adopted in Ontario in March, 1951, and it came into force on January 1, 1952. In Saskatchewan legislation was enacted on April 4, 1952, and it came into force on January 1, 1953. In British Columbia it was enacted in 1953 and came into force on January 1, 1954. This would indicate, Mr. Speaker, that there has been a growing recognition of the justice of such legislation and an increasing willingness to accept the principle and give it legal status in many countries in the world. It has already been recognized and accepted right here on the North American continent both in the United States and in Canada.
2592	HOUSE OF
Industrial Status of Women
At the thirty-third session of the ILO in 1950 the Canadian delegate, during a conference on equal pay remuneration, stated that the Canadian government was in favour of the principle and of its application to government employees, but would not be prepared to introduce legislation, giving as an excuse the difficulty of reconciling the two methods of application, that is, legal enactment and collective agreement.
As nearly as I can tell, for this reason the Canadian delegation supported the recommendation but not the convention. Throughout the consideration of the various points Canada sought to have the provisions watered down to a point where they would not necessarily be binding on the participating states. For instance, I find that in the consideration of point 4 Canada was successful in having the original wording changed so that instead of reading "each member to undertake to ensure application of the principle" it read "each member to take all practicable measures to encourage the application of the principle", and finally it was changed to read "to further, and in so far as this is in conformity with the above methods, to ensure application of the principle".
Considering that Canada wanted to take all practicable measures to encourage application of the principle, it would be interesting to know just what steps have been taken by the Canadian government in that direction since that time. I notice that at page 40 of the seventh report of the international labour conference on this subject Mr. Kaiser, who was the United States government delegate, said:
The experience of the United States showed that the principle could he accepted alike by workers and employers; that it could be translated into practice; and that its application protected established wage rates against undercutting.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: MEASURE TO REQUIRE EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have followed the remarks of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) with great care. Like her, I am very anxious to hear the opinions that may be expressed by other members of the house as the debate proceeds. This year the hon. member has introduced exactly the same bill providing for equal pay for equal work for women which she proposed last year. It was placed on the order paper very early, and one day before Christmas, when I was trying to do my homework in my office on a quiet Saturday afternoon, I read her bill just after I had read an editorial in that great paper, the Ottawa Journal. The heading of the editorial was "Not to Start Something, But-" The first paragraph reads as follows:
We have it on the authority of a Toronto columnist, who says he gets it from "the latest scientific statistics" that "more and more males are being driven out of their minds as a direct result of attempting to argue with females".
Of course the reason more and more males are being driven out of their minds is the difficulty they have in finding answers to the good arguments of the ladies. That is the position in which I find myself this afternoon.

subtopic: MEASURE TO REQUIRE EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext: If the minister will permit me, that statement has been made ever since Adam made his famous remark about the woman tempting him.

subtopic: MEASURE TO REQUIRE EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext:
Be that as it may, I am sure there is greater force in that statement just

made by my hon. friend than in the one which
1	wrote down as she was speaking a while ago, namely "that discrimination on account of wage differential has been in existence since the beginning of time". That is quite a long spell. Anyway, I recognize fully that this is one of those many occasions in life when a mere man can talk himself into quite a lot of trouble, but I should like to take advantage of the opportunity to comment on what the hon. member said in introducing the bill.
She stated that women are needed in Canada in our rapidly expanding economy, and that is certainly perfectly true. During the last 25 years Canada, as well as the rest of the western world, has seen how women can occupy practically every occupational role that in former times was considered to be the prerogative of man. What I have said also applies to this house. It is a great satisfaction to me that an increasing number of women are taking their places in the houses of parliament.
I do not want to dwell on this matter long because, as my hon. friend has said, I think the bill will provide an opportunity for a free expression of opinion on all sides of the house. However, I should like to point out in the beginning that the government of Canada, and I am very glad to say so, has followed the equal pay principle for many years in respect of its employees. That applies to governments under both parties. Rates of pay in positions under our Canadian civil service are fixed in accordance with the content of the job and are the same whether the holder of the job is a man or a woman. After a fairly long period of experience, I believe it is looked upon as an efficient method, and of course the same principle holds true as far as the rewards of members of parliament are concerned.
The equal pay laws have been outlined quite fully by the sponsor of the bill. In the United States, as she has said, there is no federal legislation although bills have been introduced on quite a number of occasions during the past eight or ten years. The basic provision of Bill No. 2 now before us is the same as that contained in the bill which was introduced, but not passed, in the United States last year. I understand from press reports that Representative Bolton of Ohio intends to sponsor such a bill in the House of Representatives this spring.
In its provisions for enforcement Bill No.
2	follows the pattern of the three provincial laws in Canada, namely Ontario, Saskatchewan, and now British Columbia since December 31. These acts provide that a woman employee who claims she is not getting equal
Industrial Status of Women pay for equal work may file a complaint with an administrative authority. This authority has the responsibility of conferring with the employer and employee, and seeking to effect a settlement. In other words I think the key idea there is the complaint, and action normally is not expected unless a complaint is lodged. I am told that the experience so far has been that very few complaints have been filed.
In the United States where some state legislation seems to place a responsibility on an administrative authority to secure compliance with the law through inspection-the key idea there seems to be inspection rather than complaints-the authorities indicate that so far there has been very little activity. It can be readily seen, I think, that no government inspector can tell whether an equal pay law is being violated simply by examining the payrolls. It means going into the job content as well, and this is particularly true where the statute requires that there shall be equal pay for comparable work. Who is to say what is comparable work, even as between two men employees? Wherever collective bargaining is feasible, and I am going to admit right away that in collective bargaining as in other spheres, though woman is a potent force which we must never underestimate, nevertheless women do not appear to be numerous in the membership of our national labour organizations, particularly those coming under federal jurisdiction.
There has been some experience in Canada in approaching the problem from the point of view of collective bargaining. Some agreements contain equal pay clauses, and others simply carry out the principle of equal pay by establishing a rate for the job which is the same whether the job is done by a man or a woman. This is the practice followed by the federal civil service commission.
My department carried out a study not merely of those people coming under federal jurisdiction but of a sample group of 1,952 collective bargaining agreements covering 343,100 workers in manufacturing. About 20 per cent of the workers were found to be covered by agreements containing equal pay clauses. Only about 3 per cent were covered by agreement which provided for lower rates for women and boys in the same job classifications as men. Most agreements had no provisions either for wage differences based on sex or for equal pay.
Very little manufacturing is subject to federal jurisdiction, of course, but I mention this study simply to indicate that there is a practical way of getting at the problem through that channel. Collective bargaining
2594	HOUSE OF
Industrial Status of Women is feasible, and is the accepted method of determining wages and working conditions in a large part of the industries subject to federal jurisdiction. In Canada we have proceeded on the assumption that there should be labour legislation when it can help to create a favourable atmosphere for collective bargaining, and that then the parties concerned should work out an agreement which sets out the terms of employment. This is certainly one of the terms of employment.
The bill we have before us is designed to make it the duty of the federal government to instruct management to do certain things relating to job classifications and pay which have been hitherto regarded as factors in collective bargaining or which have not been considered at all. As a consequence, one could conceive of a demand for legislation that would make it the duty of the federal government to instruct labour unions to do certain things relating to job classification and pay, which hitherto have been regarded as factors in the collective bargaining field.
Having said that, I do not want to give the impression that no problem exists. It has been recognized as a problem by trade unions in this country, in that the major congresses have all adopted equal pay for equal work as part of their platform of principles and at their annual conventions have discussed ways of putting it into effect. I feel it is perhaps significant that this consideration is not complete, and as an indication of that fact I point out that the four great national labour organizations have now made their annual presentations to the government and, although they have many women in their membership, have not recommended that such a bill be passed within the federal jurisdiction. I feel it is probably equally significant that the national council of women, in making their recommendations to the government, did not mention this matter. The provincial federations of trade unions have, of course, on occasion asked the provincial governments to introduce equal pay legislation.
Before advocating federal legislation in this field I think I should like to know that a specific problem existed in the industries coming within federal jurisdiction, and that it was serious enough to warrant intervention. I would want to feel that the problem appeared capable of being remedied by law. So far I do not think there has been enough evidence of such a specific problem or of the fact that this is the remedy for it.
I must say that I noted the extracts which the hon. member quoted from the statements of the Canadian representative at ILO, which


intimated no difficulty was seen in applying the principle within federal jurisdiction. I think it should be added that I am not sure there would not be certain difficulties involved if this bill became law in the federal jurisdiction, and an aggressive effort were made to enforce it. However, I can assure the hon. member that we shall keep this matter under careful study within the department and the national employment service. It might very well be, and we are looking at that, that an improvement in the provisions for women in our vocational training, counselling and placement services might gain the desired objectives more effectively than by passing a law. I cannot see my way clear to supporting this bill or recommending that a similar bill be introduced by the government at this session. This is not because I am against equal pay for women who do the same work as men. I am sure no member in this house would deny that, and it is not necessary for me to stress it.
Again I say there is a difference between attempting to bring about a remedy by law and having it carried out by collective bargaining on the one hand, and probably the more potent weapon of education on the other. It is because I am not convinced of the necessity or the desirability of trying to enforce such a law within those industries which are subject to federal labour jurisdiction that I reluctantly find I shall have to vote against my hon. friend's bill.

Mr. Chairman, there are no such recreational facilities in the building. I would emphasize that this will not be primarily an office building. Although it will contain some office space, the proposed new building is essentially a production plant designed to house technical processes of a complex kind.
The studio, for instance, must be soundproofed by means of double-shell construction. This is the case whether it is near an airport or not, and whether it is in Ottawa or Montreal. The building must have facilities to provide the laboratories with large quantities of fresh water each day at constant temperatures. Many areas must be kept air-conditioned and dust-free. Complicated electric and electronic systems must be installed. This is a specialized operation; it requires custom-made facilities, and these can be obtained efficiently only by the construction of a specially designed building, as was recommended by the parliamentary committee and others.
That is what the government are proposing to do, and we are proposing to do it in the most economical way possible.
Mr. Chairman, there are always those people who are concerned about the future of the film board. When the act was changed some three years ago fear was widely expressed in Ottawa that we were ruining the film board, despite the fact that the government made it clear that its intention was


to produce a better film board. I think the public generally is now satisfied that we have done that.
The government's intention in this instance is to produce a better board by providing it with facilities it needs in an area where it can obtain the required technical skill and creative talents to maintain that high quality of production which Canadians have come to expect from the film board. Any reduction in the amount of this vote now would in effect destroy the operation of the film board and, Mr. Chairman, the government has no intention of sitting by and seeing that done. For that reason we intend to oppose the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, we are still waiting for a word of explanation as to the choice of the site. Will the minister read to us the extracts from the three reports he has mentioned which recommended the choice of this site?
I think that question is unnecessary, Mr. Chairman.
So do I.

The Leader of the Opposition heard my statement in reply to a question he raised. I said specifically that none of the three agencies had recommended in favour of Ottawa, nor had they recommended in favour of Montreal or any other location. They simply recommended that better facilities be provided. The board itself, that independent body that the government looks to for recommendations as to policy and direction on the film board, recommended that the operating facilities of the board be moved to Montreal, and the government accepted that recommendation.
The minister misunderstood me. I asked him whether he would read us the extracts from the recommendations of the board which explained why this should be done.
I understood the Leader of the Opposition. I think I understood him correctly that he asked me to read from the reports.
No, I did not.
Oh, yes; that is what you asked for.
In any event, reports of the film board to the government are privileged documents, and I am sure hon. members-
That is the independent body.
-will assume that I am speaking correctly when I say that was their recommendation, and that the government accepted it.
Will the minister say whether there were any recommendations from any officials, other than the board, which suggested any other site?

Mr. Chairman, I think the Leader of the Opposition intends to attempt to lead me into a position where I will reveal recommendations of officials working within a government agency to the head of the agency, and I shall do no such thing.
I want the minister to disclose that there were recommendations against this.
You say so, if you know it.
By whom?

Will the minister tell the committee now that this independent body, so free of government as it is described, did not forward to the government any recommendations from the officials within the board other than those to which he has referred?
He has told you, and he is not subject to cross-examination.
The recommendations we received from the board on three separate occasions were to the effect that the operating sections of the national film board should be set up in Montreal.

Surely the minister can answer the question. Surely the minister can answer whether or not there have been received any
Supply-National Film Board recommendations other than those to which he has referred, recommendations which proposed alternative sites.
It is the national film board to whom I looked for advice when responsible to parliament, and that board recommended to me that the facilities be moved to Montreal.
Will the minister tell us what will be the total cost of the land, buildings and equipment when this is completed?

The contract cost of the building is $5,230,000. The land will cost, when settlement is completed, about $280,000. The cost of the equipment I do not know. I think my colleague will be in a better position to give an up-to-date estimate of that. I do not think the cost of new equipment will be so much. At the present time the film board is fairly well equipped. There will be cost involved in the movement of equipment to Montreal; there will doubtless be some new equipment required, but I have no estimate of what that might be.
I heard the impatient comments from those who are not interested in getting any facts.
Oh, oh.
It is all in your mind.

After all, we have had an answer now that is really merely a continuance of the answers we received on April 9 of last year: "I do not know how much it is going to be; it will not be so much." Well, how much is so much? We have just been told by the minister that one of the considerations would be the fact that there will be facilities for the production of films for television within the same area. Let us know just what it is going to cost to put in the new equipment that will be involved in bringing this operation into harmony with the other operations providing the films for television, which constitute a new operation. Can the minister not tell us that?

No, I cannot. After all, this is an estimate to cover the cost of the building in Montreal. There will be another occasion to consider the estimates of the national film board, and I suggest that would be a much more appropriate occasion on which to obtain these details.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the Minister of Public Works, because I came down here from the

Supply-National Film Board far Pacific coast with a great deal of misgiving respecting the transfer of the national film board from the capital city of Ottawa to the city of Montreal. Out on the Pacific coast we have felt, rightly or wrongly, that in the development of the federal district in and around the city of Ottawa the taxpayers of Canada were endeavouring to build a national capital.
When I left the coast on November 7 last a great number of people were concerned. What were they concerned about? They were concerned about the fact that on the one hand we were taking the taxpayers' money to develop a national capital in Ottawa, and on the other we were removing the cornerstones of that national capital and setting up the film board headquarters in the city of Montreal. That was the impression with which I came to this session of parliament. I will have to admit that until tonight, until I heard the fine explanation of the situation by the Minister of Public Works, I was labouring under a similar delusion to that of the people in my riding.
I view this situation now as one of complexity, because as I tried to get the eye of the chairman, the Leader of the Opposition rose on six different occasions. Therefore it is six to one. He is batting six hundred and I am batting only a hundred. With respect to that question, I do not mind it particularly for the simple reason that I view this situation very much like Sherlock Holmes did when he was called in to solve a very complicated situation. He said to his good friend, "Watson, I must take charge of this situation immediately because it is so complicated; I find that the window has been broken on both sides." I think the window has been broken on both sides with respect to the film board.
No windows.

We have statements without foundation, statements that have no basis in fact, rumours and frustration all over the land with respect to the national film board. We have heard tonight a review of the actual facts which prompted the government to make certain recommendations with respect to the removal of the film board.
Dispense.
That to me is a factual explanation of what has transpired.
Simple, Dr. Watson.
You are biased.

My good friend the hon. member for Peterborough says I am biased.


Possibly I am, but if I am biased I am biased on a good side. I feel that the people of Canada are vitally interested in the production of good films. I have to admit with a great deal of temerity that I am about as unarty as any unarty member in this house.
That is obvious.
Too modest.

As far as cinematography and television are concerned, I am not in the slightest concerned with them as an individual, but there are hundreds of thousands of people in my province and in the other nine provinces of Canada who look forward with a great deal of anticipation to the showing of national film board films.
In the metropolitan areas of Canada there are a thousand and one different types of amusement with which the people may amuse themselves. But let us not forget that there are many thousands of rural areas in Canada where the facilities for the handling and presenting of pictures and television are not adequate and may not be adequate for many years to come. It behooves us to do what we can, particularly for the people in those remote areas, to see to it-will this magpie chorus behind me pipe down, please?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
You have given me a derail cocktail, and I do not know where I stopped.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is where you started.

Don't worry, I will handle you later on. We have to consider the hundreds of thousands of people who do not enjoy the privileges enjoyed by those who live in the metropolitan areas from east to west in our fair domain. Those people look forward with a great deal of expectation to the presentation of national film board films in the remote areas of our land. I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, and hon. members of this committee that the spirit of Canada does not lie particularly in the metropolitan areas. The pioneering spirit that made Canada what it is today is to be found in the remote areas of this land.
It is all very well to sit back in complacency and say, "To heck with you, Joe; everything is all right as long as everything is all right with me". I was raised on a much simpler doctrine than that, to do unto others as I would that they should do unto me. I think that is the philosophy with which we should judge this great national problem today. We should consider the other fellow who is in less happy circumstances than we are.

In conclusion I want, on my own behalf and on behalf of a great number of people in British Columbia, to thank sincerely the Minister of Public Works for the fine, lucid and clear explanation he has given of this national film board problem. He and the other ministers, whether by a majority or unanimous decision of the cabinet, decided to make this change in the interests of the people of Canada. I want to leave this last closing word with you, Mr. Chairman. Under no circumstances whatsoever should any man or woman in this house judge this question upon racial or religious principles.
Oh, oh.
It must be based entirely upon that which is the best for the common weal of the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the last speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, started off by saying that he approached this question with some misgivings, but by the time he ended he had talked himself completely out of any misgivings whatsoever. His changed feelings may have been due in part to the speech which the minister made. I must say that what the minister said left me at the end with the same misgivings I had when he started.
I must also say that he made a very powerful case against the opposition, and legitimately so. I speak for myself when I say that we were lax and remiss, we were wrong; but I am not going to stay quiet because I am afraid to say I was wrong at some other time. I think the error which is being committed now is much worse than the errors which were committed by us some months ago and some years ago.
The minister has given us many reasons for the film board being moved. He has quoted reports. For instance, the Woods-Gordon company, if I remember rightly, suggested that the work of the board in Ottawa should be centralized and suitable accommodation be provided. If the minister agrees that better operating facilities should have been provided, that the film board should be operating in one building instead of in many buildings as it has in the past; if he agrees that that meant inefficiency, as it was bound to, then the government should have done something for the film board years ago when we were asking them to give some consideration to the problems of that board. But the government did nothing at all until it decided that the film board should be moved to Montreal.
Supply-National Film Board
This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition asked what were the facts upon which this decision was based. The only fact I could get out of the minister's speech concerning this decision was that in Montreal there is lots of fresh water and there is freedom from dirt and noise. I am certain that there are other areas in the country to which those facts would be equally applicable. I question profoundly the wisdom of moving the board to Montreal or any other area. When the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard expresses the hope that this matter will not be regarded in a racial or religious manner he is talking nonsense-
Nonsense to you.

I say you
are talking nonsense. No one interjected that idea until you came along.
During the course of his remarks the minister said that any reduction in this vote would destroy the effectiveness of the national film board. That is just not so. If the film board should stay in this city that fact would not reduce its effectiveness one iota compared with its effectiveness in the past. But the government has become stubborn. It has made up its mind. It has dug in its heels and said, "We are not going to budge." Yet the government's policy is not only stubborn; it is also silly. One can forgive a silly policy. After all, it is a natural manifestation. But I find it very difficult to forgive stubbornness because that is an acquired characteristic. The wedding of this manifestation and of this characteristic is usually the basis for Liberal policy; and it is not a good way, I assure hon. members, to govern this country.
The Leader of the Opposition asked for the facts on which this decision was based, but none have been forthcoming. However, there is one fact in regard to this move, and it hinges entirely upon the decision of the last commissioner of the film board. He felt it would be a good move to make and he sold a lot of people a bill of goods. I do not question that he acted honestly, nor do I question his belief that he was right. But he did sell that bill of goods to the government, and they are now either too proud or too stubborn to retreat from the position which they have taken.
This afternoon the hon. member for Ottawa West said this move came as a surprise to him. But why? After all, last year the hon. member in his position as parliamentary assistant to the Acting Prime Minister was surely on the outskirts of the government. He was surely near to government policy. He must have had some idea of what was going on.

Supply-National Film Board If this came to the hon. member as a surprise, then what sort of cabal have we existing within the government? If it came as a surprise to my hon. friend over there then it came as just as much a surprise to hon. members here. That does not mean that it becomes any more palatable.
Some arguments have been advanced for moving the film board, and the Minister of Public Works repeated some of them tonight. I simply do not agree with him any more than I suppose he agrees with me. But at least he did not use the argument I have heard so often in the past, that it is highly important from the point of view of creative capacity that the film board has to be removed from the deadening influence of the civil service atmosphere. I do not believe the atmosphere in Ottawa is as dull or as effete as many would make out.
The minister did say that it was important for the board to get into some area such as Montreal or Toronto where there was a pool of creative talent. But may I remind the minister that Montreal and Toronto are not the only areas in this country in which there is creative talent. One has only to listen to the radio to find that there is as much creative talent in Winnipeg or Vancouver or in other areas across the country. I think it is true to say that the best films produced by the film board have not used professional talent but ordinary run of the mill Canadians, ordinary men, women and children; and the film board does not depend upon a pool of creative talent such as the minister suggests in order to do its best work. I admit that in Montreal and Toronto there are professional actors, but I do not believe they are a necessity to the operations of the film board.
The minister mentioned television. Television is important, and the part which the film board can play in television is perhaps very important. But we can make no greater mistake than to assume that the primary task of the film board is to act as an adjunct to the C.B.C. in producing films for television. There is a vast difference between the sort of work we expect from the film board, which is interpreting Canada to Canadians, and the work being done on television. Television is something which is evanescent, something like the reports which are made by journalists for newspapers. They are written, printed and then disappear from the ken of man. The sort of film we expect from the film board is something which is going to be of more lasting importance, which will have some effect and which will still be worth seeing two or three years from now.


It has been suggested that it would be advisable to have the film board administration decentralized, but this is a suggestion which I simply cannot understand. What is going to happen is this. The working section of the film board is going to be near Montreal and the administrative offices of the film board are going to be in Ottawa. How in the name of business or sanity can one expect the film board to adequately administer the corporation without being much nearer the scene of operations? That sort of arrangement does not add up to sense.
The government has loaded the incoming commissioner with a tremendous incubus which may conceivably weigh him down. I do not believe it is a fair proposition. He had no say in the policy, but he happens to have inherited the policy of his predecessor who, in turn, sold what I call a bill of goods to the government.
Another factor which must be borne in mind is that the film board must maintain the closest liaison with government departments. What sort of bill for travelling expenses are we going to accumulate on behalf of the film board personnel when they move to Montreal if they have repeatedly to get in touch with government departments in this city? Research has to be carried out which can only be conducted in the national capital, for the facts and figures and the kind of information they require will have to be found here. That will mean they will have to commute between Montreal and Ottawa, and one can easily imagine the kind of bill we will have to meet. In addition, how can the commissioner possibly keep a finger on everything, and maintain efficiency in Montreal if he has to spend most of his time in Ottawa? However, the government feels that the commissioner ought to be here, and perhaps in Montreal we will have some other administrative group.
One of the big problems is going to be the fact that several hundred employees of the film board are going to move. It may be unpleasant, but hundreds have to do that in other employment. One can sympathize with them, but it is not an insuperable problem. A greater argument to my mind and of greater importance is that many members of the film board, rather than uproot themselves here and rather than go to another province- and I do not care which province it is-might decide to leave the film board. It is conceivable that many of the brighter people in the film board would rather stay here in the hope of getting other jobs or go into the professional production of films in this city, and they may leave the board.

As I said before, the last commissioner came to the conclusion that the move to Montreal would be a good idea. He sold this idea to a great number of people in this city. He sold the idea to the editor of the Ottawa Citizen, though let it be said for him that he came out in his own paper and admitted that he had been sold the idea, that he now realizes the idea is not as good as he first thought, and that he has changed his mind on the subject.
The government has accepted this recommendation, and this is the only fact which has been given to us. Now the government has become stubborn. It feels that its prestige is at stake, and it is now resolved not to budge. If I may put the matter colloquially I would sum it up in this way, Mr. Chairman. The last commissioner laid an egg and the administration sitting over there has hatched something pretty horrible.

In speaking to the amendment I should like to suggest that the Minister of Public Works made an excellent case for the moving of the film board, so far as the government's view is concerned. I believe he has sold us on the idea that the film board should be moved, but I do not know that he has sold us on where it should be moved. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard suggested that there were other places, but tonight he has been so favourably impressed as to believe that Montreal must be the place and Montreal alone. The hon. member for Winnipeg North has suggested that Montreal and Toronto are not the only places of culture in Canada. I believe that truer words were never spoken. In Winnipeg and Vancouver we have two of the finest cultural centres in all Canada.
Why do we have to centralize everything in the east? If we are going to move something, let us move something westward for a change. I happen to be the member for New Westminster, but I do not necessarily suggest that New Westminster must be the place. The Minister of Public Works did say that a bilingual centre must be chosen. Very close to the city of New Westminster, in the town of Maillardville, we have one of the finest groups of French-Canadian people that one could find. They may not be as cultured as those of the far east-
Far more.

-but at least we have a bilingual situation there. If it is so simple to move the film board to the city of Montreal, would it not be just as simple to move some of our people of French culture to the far west, to the city of Vancouver, let us say? We have
Supply-National Film Board the trees, the mountains, the sea and everything else that could be desired for the filming of beautiful pictures. If it does become the policy of the government to start decentralizing things, then I suggest that the government should get up and say so. Let them "tell the people that they are going to decentralize. Let them say that they are going to move the Department of Agriculture to the province of Alberta or to Saskatchewan. The province of British Columbia deserves more public works in proportion to the taxation it has paid in the past 20 years than any other province, so let them move the Department of Public Works to the Pacific coast. Let us decentralize these departments.
Coming back to the particular problem of the film board, it has taken the government a matter of three years, from 1950 to 1953, to sell itself the idea that it is necessary to move the board to Montreal. The Leader of the Opposition asked a most pertinent question about other recommendations, but we did not get a satisfactory answer. I think the people of Canada are entitled to know whether there are any other places in Canada that should have the privilege of at least expecting that the film board might be moved to their particular localities.
Reference was made to the matter of television, but I do not think that should be considered in the same light as the production of films for the people of Canada. As I understand it, the purpose of the film board is to sell Canada to Canadians through films produced by the board. The project is an excellent one, but if we are going to sell Canada to Canadians through the film board then the question of television is rather irrelevant, because television sells itself with the Hollywood type of picture that seems so desirable in so far as the public are concerned. Wrestling matches and things of that type are a lot more appealing to the public than the Kitimat project, for instance.
I would say that the biggest problem the film board must solve today is the matter of public relations between the government and the people of Canada. For instance, I saw a very interesting film on the Kitimat project. I think any Canadian who sees that film will understand that the government is definitely trying to assist in the building up of Canada. That happens to be a particular project. I would go so far as to suggest that if that is the problem confronting the board, then what is wrong with keeping the film board in Ottawa? Why must we go to Montreal to visit the central offices of the film board? Why must we go to Hull to see the printing bureau? When I come to the

Supply-National Film Board capital city of Canada I do not expect to have to run all over the rest of Canada to visit the various government offices.
If we are going to have centralization, then let it be here in our national capital. If it is necessary let us build a pentagon, or something similar to what has been constructed in the United States, to house all our important departments. So far as I am concerned I have not heard a plausible reason why the offices of the film board should be moved from Ottawa to Montreal, Vancouver or any other place in Canada. I suggest that the problem should be examined very closely and carefully. If we are going to decentralize the departments of government we should make a particular point to tell the people of Canada. The government should be honest about it and tell the people that for protective purposes, or whatever the reason may be, they are going to decentralize and place various offices right across Canada, so that if you want to see someone about a particular project you may have to travel from one end of the country to the other.
I suggest that might not be a bad idea at that. Members of parliament might become more familiar with the rest of Canada if, for example, a certain office was on the west coast and another one was in Newfoundland. We might see some members when they came to the far west, and have the privilege of explaining our problems to them. I am sure the hon. member from Newfoundland who commended this move a moment ago would be just as happy to see some of us come to Newfoundland so he could explain to us the problems with respect to fishing and other matters.
I do not wish to speak at great length on this particular problem, and I hope I have not tired you, Mr. Chairman. But the spirit of Canada must prevail, the spirit of either centralization or decentralization. In this particular instance the Canadian people have every right to know exactly what is the full truth of the story. We should have a clear explanation, but up to now I would say it is as clear as mud.

Mr. Chairman, during the discussion tonight some reference has been made to the committee on the national film board of 1952. When the minister referred to that committee, it seemed to me that he was suggesting that there was unanimous approval of the idea of shifting the national film board headquarters to Montreal. It was my privilege to sit as a member on that committee, and as I listened to the presentation of the then chairman of the board, Mr. Irwin,

it was not my impression that the committee generally agreed with the idea that the location of the film board should be changed from Ottawa to Montreal. In fact my sentiments were just the opposite, and I believe that if other members of the committee take part in this discussion they will reveal similar sentiments.
I must also admit that my sentiments have not been changed by anything that has been said in the discussion thus far, either by the minister or by anyone else who has spoken in favour of the move. Rather I would agree with the hon. member for Ottawa West who put forth an excellent case here this afternoon for the retention of the film board activities in the capital city.
During the minister's remarks he made some reference to a question I asked during the deliberations of the committee. The question was something like this: Why was the film board going to be moved from Ottawa to Montreal? If the minister had continued reading the evidence he would have revealed that I expressed ideas similar to those which have just been put forward by the hon. member for New Westminster. If it was necessary to change the location of the film board, why not move it to some other part of Canada which could provide adequate facilities for carrying on the operations of the board? I shall pursue that point further toward the conclusion of my remarks.
At this stage in my discussion I want to point out that there are two phases, as I see them, of national film board operations. In the first instance we have the basic task of production. As I have listened to the discussion it has seemed to me that hon. members from all sides of the house have indicated agreement that the national film board has done an excellent job under rather difficult circumstances, in providing educational and documentary films that emphasize the Canadian viewpoint. There seems to be general agreement on that conclusion.
Just as important as the task of producing films is the job of distribution. When the Minister of Public Works indicated that there had been a decrease of some 200 employees engaged in film board operations, it occurred to me immediately that this reduction in personnel had taken place not on the production side of film-making but rather on the distribution side. Before I came to this house it was my privilege to be quite closely associated with the distribution of films through our local film council in the city of Brandon.
I recall that just after the war there was a substantial national film board staff located in the Winnipeg regional office. This staff

was drastically reduced in about 1948. The reduction in staff took place among the field men who were working in the rural areas carrying on the important task of bringing documentary and educational films to the people in the relatively isolated sections of Canada, those who could most benefit from them.
At that time, in 1948, when the reduction in staff occurred-which I have just learned this evening came as the result of government policy at that time-the work of film distribution was rather sadly dislocated. The problem has been overcome by voluntary action at the local level, so that today film distribution is largely out of the hands of film board agencies. We find that most of the work of distribution in the rural areas is being handled by university extension departments. Only this winter the University of Manitoba followed the general trend and assumed complete responsibility for the distribution not only of national film board pictures but also films produced by any other agency in Canada, as well as from the many other sources of supply that are available outside Canada. There is no responsibility devolving upon the national film board in that regard at all.
Then, too, I think one of the most encouraging developments in this effort to bring good films to the people is the increase in voluntary action by local councils. It became necessary to fill the gap that was left by the sudden evacuation of the national film board, and during the past five or six years almost every area in the province from which I come has succeeded in gathering together a group of public-minded citizens who are enthusiastically taking care of this problem of distribution. Not only do they provide facilities for film distribution but they carry on considerable propaganda through the local press and through the conduct of film festivals, and in addition by buying their own projection equipment. Formerly this equipment was supplied through national film board channels. Through the appeals for funds to obtain sufficient money to provide the equipment, general interest in the viewing of worth-while films is stimulated among service club groups and other groups in that particular community.
We should remember also that various organizations representing important groups in the country are solidly behind the program for bringing good films to the local communities. I need only refer to such activities as citizens' forums, the farm forum, labour organizations and farm organizations to indicate that each one of these groups has made an outstanding contribution to the
Supply-National Film Board success of the films for the masses program which has made such headway during postwar years. I would suggest to those responsible that if we are going to have any objectivity at all in this government-sponsored film production program, the closest liaison should be maintained with those organizations representing all cross-sections of Canadian public opinion.
The question has already been put to the minister tonight as to the membership of the advisory board that is supposed to have made the recommendation for the move to Montreal. Several times during the contribution by the Minister of Public Works he said that the final decision was based on the recommendations of the board of directors of the national film board. I would be intrigued to know whether there is a representative, for example of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the C.C.L., the T.L.C., or other organizations on that board, because I think if you are going to keep in touch with the real needs of the community in so far as film production is concerned, that can be done only through the closest possible co-operation with these groups.
Whenever a government assumes direct responsibility for mass media of communication, no matter how deeply saturated in democratic traditions that government may be there is always the danger that the mass media will be used to manipulate public opinion for political purposes. The very fact that the national film board moved forward so rapidly during the war is indicative of the success that can be achieved by the use of this media in influencing public opinion. I remember the impact that the outstanding "Canada Carries On" series made upon the people of Canada in wartime, as the national film board endeavoured to stimulate interest and enthusiasm in respect of the war effort.
The matter of distribution is largely out of the hands of national film board officials, and has moved to voluntary groups, consisting largely of film councils in co-operation with university extension departments. I think that is all to the good.
To bring my remarks to a conclusion-
Hear, hear.

Some hon. members on the other side say "hear, hear". They do not like this. To bring my remarks to a conclusion I wish to refer again briefly to the recommendation I made during the hearings of the committee back in 1952. At that time I asked, if it was necessary to change the location of the film board, why a city like Winnipeg could not be considered. At the time I put forward this suggestion it was

Supply-National Film Board regarded as facetious by members of the committee. But, judging from the reasons for the move given by the minister tonight, I think the capital city of the keystone province has all the qualifications necessary to carry on an adequate film production program.
First of all the explanation was put forward that only Toronto and Montreal provide sufficient talent resources. It was my privilege to visit the present building housing thq national film board-I believe it is down on John street-and, moving through the various departments, it was almost like old home week, because located there were many westerners who had been caught up in the great migration from the prairies. This is a subject often discussed in the house, the problem of rural-urban migration. As I say, it was almost like old home week.
The city of Winnipeg is unique as a cultural centre in Canada. In addition to its geographical location in the centre of Canada it is the home of the Royal Winnipeg Ballet, the outstanding activity of its kind in the dominion. It boasts the world's greatest musical festival, one that is recognized in other countries outside Canada. It has an outstanding symphony orchestra. Its theatrical productions are featured regularly on drama programs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. One could mention many individual artists-and I think particularly of Donna Grescoe, the great Canadian violinist -who had their origin in the city of Winnipeg, in the keystone province.
The argument has been offered here that the main emphasis by the national film board is to appeal to the rural audience. I understand that 20 per cent of the production budget will go into the manufacture of films for consumption by our rural audiences in isolated centres. I cannot see for the life of me how operating in Montreal is going to cater to the group who most need these additional cultural facilities, namely our rural audience.
The only talent that seems to exist in abundance in the city of Montreal is a superabundance of Liberal members. And-
Hear, hear.

Looking at the situation logically, without emotion or bias, it seems to me that the presence of this sort of talent might have had more to do with the decision than the cultural talent to which our attention has been directed. One further word regarding the suitability of other parts of Canada as compared with Montreal.
Is the hon. member serious in his assertion that Winnipeg would provide as good talent of a bilingual nature as can be provided in Montreal?

I was coming to that. Winnipeg is unique as a prairie city in that cultural duality is strongly represented there in the city of St. Boniface, which has all the characteristics of French-speaking Canada and, in addition, has that unique exuberance and creativity that is peculiar to the western provinces of our great dominion. And so from every aspect-
Ten o'clock.

I shall be finished in two or three minutes. If we must shift, must we think only in terms of Ontario or Quebec? Let us think in terms of other parts of Canada which merit consideration. If we are really going to develop Canada as a strong nation among the family of nations in the modern world, we must think in terms broader than the city of Toronto or the city of Montreal.
Returning to the main topic for discussion, I emphasize as strongly as I can that I am vigorously opposed to any move of national film board operations from the city of Ottawa. We have established our national capital here. The recognition of Ottawa as a national capital is gradually being accepted in other parts of Canada and the world. Such a move is definitely not in the best national interests.
Apparently the hon. member has changed his mind.

This is my last sentence. I also suggest that the provision of adequate facilities for the national film board could be done with a much more economical expenditure than that indicated in the estimate.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
